analysis.evidence: אַבְרָם is the subject. מִמִּצְרַיִם gives his point of departure, Egypt, and הַנֶּגְבָּה gives his destination, the Negev. The verb describes Abram’s journey up from Egypt.
analysis.morphology: The prefixed conjunction וַ combines with the shortened Qal imperfect יַּעַל to form a third-person masculine singular wayyiqtol agreeing with אַבְרָם.

draft.change: Link the existing Abram article to אבה through its father element and add Genesis 12:4 as an example.
draft.definition: Abram, son of Terah, later named Abraham. The name means “exalted father.”
draft.evidence: Genesis 12:4 repeats the name אַבְרָם when giving Abram’s age at departure. The name’s אָב element belongs to Haqor’s אבה article.

analysis.evidence: אַבְרָם names the subject of וַיַּעַל, “went up.” Abram went up from Egypt toward the Negev, accompanied by his wife and Lot.
analysis.morphology: Hebrew personal name with no prefix or suffix.
analysis.sense: Abram, the son of Terah later named Abraham

analysis.evidence: וַיַּעַל אַבְרָם מִמִּצְרַיִם says that Abram went up from Egypt. The directional form הַנֶּגְבָּה gives his destination, the Negev, and Egypt is his point of departure.
analysis.morphology: The prefixed preposition מִן means “from.” Its nun assimilates to the initial mem of the proper name מִצְרַיִם, as the dagesh shows.

analysis.evidence: After וַיַּעַל אַבְרָם מִמִּצְרַיִם (‘Abram went up from Egypt’), הוּא refers back to Abram. The phrase הוּא וְאִשְׁתּוֹ (‘he and his wife’) places him first in the list of those who went up together.
analysis.morphology: Independent third-person masculine singular personal pronoun.

analysis.evidence: In הוּא וְאִשְׁתּוֹ, “he and his wife,” הוּא refers to Abram, and the possessive suffix identifies the woman accompanying him from Egypt as his wife.
analysis.morphology: The conjunction וְ precedes the feminine singular construct noun אִשְׁתּ־. The third-person masculine singular suffix וֹ means “his.”

analysis.evidence: The relative clause אֲשֶׁר לוֹ “that belonged to him” limits כָל to Abram’s possessions. The phrase means “and all that he owned.”
analysis.morphology: The conjunction וְ “and” prefixes כָל, a masculine singular noun in the construct state.

analysis.evidence: In וְכָל אֲשֶׁר לוֹ, “and all that belonged to him,” אֲשֶׁר introduces the relative clause modifying כָל. The possessive לוֹ refers to Abram.
analysis.morphology: Uninflected Hebrew relative particle without a prefix or suffix.

draft.change: Add Genesis 13:1 as an example of the existing le-belongs sense of Hebrew לְ.
draft.definition: לְ marks the person to whom something belongs.
draft.evidence: Genesis 13:1 repeats כָּל אֲשֶׁר לוֹ from Genesis 12:20. In both verses the suffix refers to Abram.

analysis.evidence: In וְכָל אֲשֶׁר לוֹ, “and all that belonged to him,” לוֹ is the predicate of the relative clause. Its suffix identifies Abram as the owner. Genesis 12:20 uses the same phrase for what Abram took with him.
analysis.morphology: The preposition לְ takes the third-person masculine singular pronominal suffix וֹ, referring to Abram.
analysis.sense: Marks the possessor in a clause expressing ownership.

evidence.note: The genealogy lists Abram and Haran among Terah’s sons and names Lot as Haran’s son.
וְלוֹט עִמּוֹ names Lot as a companion of Abram on the journey from Egypt.

article.name: לוֹט
article.summary: Lot was the son of Haran, Abram’s brother. He accompanied Abram from Egypt toward the Negeb. The meaning of his name is uncertain.

draft.change: Add a personal-name article for לוֹט. The derivation of the name is uncertain.
draft.definition: Lot, son of Haran and nephew of Abram.
draft.evidence: Genesis 11:27 names Haran as Lot’s father. Genesis 13:1 names Lot as Abram’s companion on the journey from Egypt.

analysis.evidence: וְלוֹט עִמּוֹ means ‘and Lot with him’. It names Lot among those who went up from Egypt with Abram. Genesis 12:5 identifies him as the son of Abram’s brother.
analysis.morphology: The conjunction וְ ‘and’ prefixes the masculine personal name לוֹט.

analysis.evidence: וַיַּעַל אַבְרָם מִמִּצְרַיִם says that Abram went up from Egypt. הַנֶּגְבָּה gives the destination of that journey, the Negev.
analysis.morphology: The definite article הַ precedes a masculine singular absolute noun. The final directional ה marks the destination.
